questions.Source/Guideline: Diagnosis and Treatment of Non-Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer: AUA/SUO Guideline
questions.Question: A fit woman has completely resected multifocal high-risk high-grade Ta bladder tumors, muscle present, no perforation, and BCG supply is available. Which intravesical plan is most appropriate?
questions.Explanation: Option A is correct. High-risk Ta urothelial carcinoma is an indication for a six-week induction course of BCG when BCG is available and the patient can receive it. Option B is incorrect because high-grade Ta disease has enough recurrence and progression risk to warrant induction intravesical therapy. Option C is incorrect because immediate radical cystectomy is not routine for a completely resected treatment-naive Ta tumor. Option D is incorrect because nadofaragene is used in selected BCG-unresponsive settings rather than before BCG exposure. Option E is incorrect because surveillance alone undertreats high-grade Ta risk. Teaching point: The key branch is BCG availability and risk group, not the noninvasive Ta label alone. Source: American Urological Association. Diagnosis and Treatment of Non-Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer: AUA/SUO Guideline.

questions.Source/Guideline: Diagnosis and Treatment of Non-Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer: AUA/SUO Guideline
questions.Question: A patient has high-risk BCG-unresponsive NMIBC with persistent carcinoma in situ after adequate BCG. He is unwilling to undergo cystectomy. Which bladder-sparing option is guideline-concordant to discuss?
questions.Option D: Nadofaragene firadenovec or another alternative intravesical therapy
questions.Option E: Pelvic radiation as routine NMIBC salvage
questions.Explanation: Option D is correct. For a patient with high-risk BCG-unresponsive NMIBC who is unwilling or unfit for cystectomy, the AUA/SUO guideline supports discussing bladder-sparing options such as clinical trial enrollment, alternative intravesical therapy including nadofaragene firadenovec or gemcitabine-docetaxel, and pembrolizumab for carcinoma in situ. Option A is incorrect because persistent BCG-unresponsive disease is not managed by simply extending BCG alone. Option B is incorrect because high-risk persistent CIS should not be observed until progression. Option C is incorrect because a single postoperative instillation is a perioperative recurrence-reduction step, not salvage for BCG-unresponsive CIS. Option E is incorrect because routine pelvic radiation is not the guideline bladder-sparing salvage pathway for NMIBC. Teaching point: BCG-unresponsive high-risk NMIBC forces a cystectomy discussion, but cystectomy-ineligible or refusing patients still have defined bladder-sparing salvage options. Source: American Urological Association. Diagnosis and Treatment of Non-Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer: AUA/SUO Guideline.

questions.Source/Guideline: Salvage Therapy for Prostate Cancer: AUA/ASTRO/SUO Guideline
questions.Question: A man has pelvic nodal recurrence after prostatectomy, no distant disease, and salvage treatment is planned. Which approach should be offered?
questions.Option A: Pelvic lymphadenectomy as a proven curative substitute
questions.Option B: ADT plus salvage RT to the prostate bed and pelvic nodes
questions.Option C: Docetaxel with salvage RT and ADT
questions.Option D: Ignore nodal disease during radiation planning
questions.Explanation: Option B is correct. Pelvic nodal recurrence after radical prostatectomy should prompt an offer of ADT plus salvage radiation to the prostate bed and pelvic lymph nodes. Option A is incorrect because salvage pelvic lymphadenectomy has uncertain oncologic benefit and is not the standard substitute in this setting. Option C is incorrect because docetaxel should not be added to salvage RT and ADT for this indication. Option D is incorrect because visible pelvic nodal disease should be incorporated into treatment planning. Option E is incorrect because BCG is bladder-directed therapy. Teaching point: Regional recurrence after prostatectomy is a combined local-regional radiation and systemic-hormonal decision. Source: American Urological Association. Salvage Therapy for Prostate Cancer: AUA/ASTRO/SUO Guideline.
questions.Distractor Verdict: Choices distinguish nodal salvage RT planning from surgery, chemotherapy escalation, and irrelevant bladder therapy.
questions.Source Verdict: Supported by the public AUA salvage therapy guideline.
questions.Verification Findings: Claude flag resolved: AUA Salvage Therapy Statement 26 supports ADT plus salvage RT to prostate bed and pelvic nodes for pelvic nodal recurrence after primary RP; docetaxel is not the offered regional-recurrence pathway.

questions.Source/Guideline: Medical Management of Kidney Stones: AUA Guideline
questions.Question: A first-time calcium stone former has a solitary kidney and wants prevention beyond general advice. Which evaluation is most guideline-concordant?
questions.Option A: No testing unless a second stone forms
questions.Option B: One or two 24-hour urine collections on a random diet
questions.Option D: Bone scan to classify stone composition
questions.Explanation: Option B is correct. Additional metabolic testing is appropriate for high-risk first-time stone formers and recurrent stone formers, and it consists of one or two 24-hour urine collections on a random diet with core lithogenic measurements. Option A is incorrect because solitary kidney status makes recurrence prevention more consequential. Option C is incorrect because cystoscopy does not measure stone-risk chemistry. Option D is incorrect because bone scan does not classify urinary stone composition. Option E is incorrect because antibiotics do not replace metabolic evaluation. Teaching point: A first stone can still deserve full metabolic evaluation when the recurrence consequence is high. Source: American Urological Association. Medical Management of Kidney Stones: AUA Guideline.
questions.Distractor Verdict: Distractors test imaging, cystoscopy, and empiric treatment versus metabolic evaluation.
questions.Source Verdict: Supported by the public AUA kidney stones guideline.
questions.Verification Findings: First-time stone former with solitary kidney is a high-risk context where metabolic testing is appropriate.
questions.Verified Sources: AUA Medical Management of Kidney Stones: https://www.auanet.org/guidelines-and-quality/guidelines/kidney-stones-medical-mangement-guideline

questions.Source/Guideline: Medical Management of Kidney Stones: AUA Guideline
questions.Question: A recurrent stone former starts a prevention plan and has small nonobstructing renal stones under surveillance. What follow-up best assesses stone activity?
questions.Option A: No imaging if flank pain is absent
questions.Option C: Periodic imaging with KUB, renal ultrasound, or low-dose CT
questions.Option D: Urine cytology as the primary growth test
questions.Explanation: Option C is correct. Follow-up of medical stone prevention should include periodic imaging based on stone activity to assess growth or new stone formation, using modalities such as plain abdominal imaging, renal ultrasonography, or low-dose CT. Option A is incorrect because asymptomatic stones can grow or recur. Option B is incorrect because cystoscopy does not monitor renal stone burden. Option D is incorrect because cytology evaluates urothelial malignancy risk, not stone activity. Option E is incorrect because bone scan is not a renal stone surveillance tool. Teaching point: Stone prevention is judged by both urine chemistry and actual stone burden over time. Source: American Urological Association. Medical Management of Kidney Stones: AUA Guideline.
questions.Distractor Verdict: Choices distinguish stone activity surveillance from unrelated endoscopy or symptom-only follow-up.
questions.Source Verdict: Supported by the public AUA kidney stones guideline.
questions.Verification Findings: Periodic imaging is appropriate to assess stone growth or new stone formation during prevention follow-up.
questions.Verified Sources: AUA Medical Management of Kidney Stones: https://www.auanet.org/guidelines-and-quality/guidelines/kidney-stones-medical-mangement-guideline

questions.Source/Guideline: The AUA/SUFU Guideline on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Idiopathic Overactive Bladder
questions.Question: An older man with a working AUS has urgency incontinence despite mirabegron, PVR 0 mL, no erosion, and urodynamic detrusor overactivity. What is a reasonable next OAB therapy?
questions.Explanation: Option D is correct. For idiopathic OAB symptoms that persist despite medication, minimally invasive therapies such as intradetrusor botulinum toxin can be offered after appropriate evaluation and counseling. Option A is incorrect because the stem supports urgency incontinence rather than recurrent stress incontinence from AUS failure. Option B is incorrect because the device is functioning and overfilling the balloon risks urethral harm. Option C is incorrect because chronic urethral catheterization is not routine OAB escalation. Option E is incorrect because cystectomy is not an OAB treatment. Teaching point: Incontinence after AUS requires separating device failure from detrusor-driven urgency before escalating therapy. Source: American Urological Association. The AUA/SUFU Guideline on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Idiopathic Overactive Bladder.
questions.Distractor Verdict: Distractors distinguish OAB procedural escalation from AUS revision, antibiotics, and cancer therapy.
questions.Explanation Verdict: Explanation addresses retention and AUS-specific distractors.
questions.Source Verdict: Supported by the public AUA/SUFU idiopathic OAB guideline.
questions.Verification Findings: Intradetrusor botulinum toxin is reasonable in a carefully selected refractory OAB patient with low PVR and no AUS erosion.

questions.Source/Guideline: The AUA/SUFU Guideline on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Idiopathic Overactive Bladder
questions.Question: A woman with bothersome idiopathic OAB wants a non-drug option, wants to avoid retention risk, and can attend repeated office visits. Which option best fits?
questions.Option C: OnabotulinumtoxinA injection to avoid retention risk
questions.Explanation: Option E is correct. Percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation is a minimally invasive OAB therapy that can fit a patient prioritizing reversibility and avoiding retention risk while accepting repeated visits. Option A is incorrect because augmentation cystoplasty is a rare last-resort option for severe refractory disease. Option B is incorrect because chronic catheterization is not routine treatment for idiopathic OAB. Option C is incorrect because intradetrusor botulinum toxin can be effective but carries urinary retention and PVR-monitoring considerations, which conflicts with her priority to avoid retention risk. Option D is incorrect because cytology does not select OAB therapy. Teaching point: OAB procedural counseling should match therapy burden and adverse-effect profile to patient priorities. Source: American Urological Association. The AUA/SUFU Guideline on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Idiopathic Overactive Bladder.

questions.Question: A high-risk microhematuria patient needs upper-tract evaluation but has an iodinated contrast allergy. What is the preferred imaging substitute if feasible?
questions.Explanation: Option A is correct. High-risk microhematuria requires cystoscopy plus axial upper-tract imaging; when multiphasic CT urography is contraindicated, MR urography may be used if feasible. Option B is incorrect because cytology alone does not evaluate the renal cortex or urothelium. Option C is incorrect because cystoscopy evaluates the bladder but not the upper tracts. Option D is incorrect because bone scan does not evaluate hematuria sources. Option E is incorrect because chemotherapy is not a diagnostic test. Teaching point: The high-risk hematuria imaging pathway has a hierarchy: CT urography, then MR urography, then retrograde pyelography with noncontrast imaging or ultrasound when both are contraindicated. Source: American Urological Association. Microhematuria: AUA/SUFU Guideline.
questions.Distractor Verdict: Distractors distinguish CT contraindication hierarchy from incomplete imaging.
questions.Explanation Verdict: Explanation clearly gives the fallback imaging sequence.
questions.Source Verdict: Supported by the public AUA/SUFU microhematuria guideline.
questions.Verification Findings: MR urography is the preferred substitute when CT urography is contraindicated and MR is feasible.

questions.Question: A patient had a negative risk-based microhematuria evaluation. Repeat urinalysis one year later is negative, and no new symptoms are present. What is reasonable?
questions.Explanation: Option C is correct. After a prior negative hematuria evaluation, a subsequent negative urinalysis allows clinicians to discontinue further microhematuria evaluation. Option A is incorrect because indefinite CT urography creates harm without guideline support. Option B is incorrect because repeat cystoscopy is not required when the repeat urinalysis is negative and symptoms have not changed. Option D is incorrect because serial urine markers do not replace risk-based follow-up. Option E is incorrect because BCG is bladder cancer therapy, not hematuria prophylaxis. Teaching point: Hematuria follow-up is not endless when the risk-based workup and repeat urinalysis are both negative. Source: American Urological Association. Microhematuria: AUA/SUFU Guideline.
questions.Distractor Verdict: Choices distinguish negative follow-up from unnecessary cystoscopy, antibiotics, or surveillance escalation.
questions.Source Verdict: Supported by the public AUA/SUFU microhematuria guideline.
questions.Verification Findings: After a negative evaluation and negative repeat urinalysis, further microhematuria evaluation may be discontinued.

questions.Source/Guideline: Recurrent Uncomplicated Urinary Tract Infections in Women: AUA/CUA/SUFU Guideline
questions.Question: A premenopausal woman has culture-proven recurrent cystitis episodes clustered after intercourse. She wants prevention and accepts limited antibiotic exposure. What strategy best fits?
questions.Option A: Routine cystoscopy before each intercourse-associated episode
questions.Option B: Daily fluoroquinolone prophylaxis as the default
questions.Option C: Post-coital antibiotic prophylaxis after shared decision-making
questions.Option E: Upper-tract imaging before any prevention plan
questions.Explanation: Option C is correct. For women with recurrent uncomplicated UTIs temporally related to intercourse, post-coital antibiotic prophylaxis can reduce recurrence while limiting antibiotic exposure compared with continuous daily prophylaxis. Option A is incorrect because cystoscopy is not repeated around each uncomplicated episode. Option B is incorrect because broad daily fluoroquinolone prophylaxis is poor stewardship when a narrower timed strategy fits the trigger. Option D is incorrect because asymptomatic bacteriuria should not drive treatment. Option E is incorrect because routine upper-tract imaging is not required for the index recurrent uncomplicated UTI pattern. Teaching point: Recurrent UTI prevention should match the recurrence phenotype; sex-associated episodes can be managed with targeted post-coital prophylaxis rather than default continuous therapy. Source: American Urological Association. Recurrent Uncomplicated Urinary Tract Infections in Women: AUA/CUA/SUFU Guideline.
questions.Accuracy Verdict: Guideline-concordant and source-supported after duplicate concept replacement.
questions.Distractor Verdict: Distractors separate post-coital prophylaxis from cystoscopy, fluoroquinolone overuse, and asymptomatic bacteriuria treatment.
questions.Source Verdict: Supported by the public AUA/CUA/SUFU recurrent UTI guideline.
questions.Verification Findings: Replaced duplicate vaginal-estrogen recurrent UTI concept with post-coital prophylaxis for intercourse-associated recurrent cystitis.
